We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Along the way, Codex also generated those anatomical illustrations showing where each organ sits in the human body, and even created the interactive hotspot markers that explain different parts of every organ. It handled all of that. The process wasn't exactly one shot, but it also wasn't difficult. You just have to do it step by step. It genuinely felt like building something that could make learning anatomy much more engaging. The inspiration came from @DilumSanjaya 's 3D animal plant cell project. No, the answer is simple: their model size is ridiculously small compared to its performance. It's 10x smaller than Opus, and 5x smaller than Sonnet. If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

It's not time to slow down but to accelerate! The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture! If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have. We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. To get there, we need three things in my opinion: - Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks - Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them - Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger. And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more. It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

Yes, LLM architectures are getting a little more complicated

The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

great write up, evals are hard! here are 2 broad buckets we use to evaluate agents: 1. Measure the State of the World 2. Agent as a Judge on the Trajectory 1. Measure the state of the environment before and after the Agent does the Task. @harborframework and containerized Evals make this easier. The agent thinks in operating in a real world and we need to set up that world (files, installed tools, security boundaries, instructions) such that it mirrors what the agent will do in the real world. Every action the agent takes alters the world in some way. And success on a task means running a verification step on the final state of the world after the agent is done to see if this state corresponds to a successful pass. The tricky thing here is calibrating when the agent produces a final state that’s technically correct but your verifier didn’t forsee - you often want to allow this to pass or make sure the correct end state is capturable by your verifier. 2. Judge the trajectory -> Correctness is not the only factor - cost, latency, interpretability matter too. Those require understanding the action space The right answer is a good signal, but if the agent got there by cheating the Task then that means our agent is misaligned AND our task is bad because it allows cheating. If the agent is inefficient with cost/tokens, then that’s a signal that we may need to imbue more priors to help it find the correct trajectory (could be better prompting) we’ll be doing a bunch more educational content and open sourcing our tooling, reach out if there’s anything you want to see in particular! this should be accessible and easy for every team to do! Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch) Why is evaluating agents so difficult relative to evaluating a standard LLM? An LLM generates a single response to a prompt. An agent instead interacts with an environment by reasoning, calling tools, observing the results, and repeating. Rather than evaluating a single output, we are evaluating a full trajectory for a long horizon problem. Outcome & environment. Success is usually determined by the final outcome. Instead of checking the agent’s output, however, we usually check the actual state of the environment after a trajectory completes. For example: - A coding agent can say it fixed a bug but still fail test cases. - A personal assistant could say “your flight has been booked!”, but we don’t know if this is true until we check the booking database. The environment plays a huge role in the evaluation process. For example, we need a stable environment that does not change over time in order to run reliable evals, and we need this environment to be efficient so that evals can be run efficiently. Additionally, the environment must be realistic and expose the proper harness / tools for the agent to be effective. Environment state. The final answer is only one part of the evaluation. We also need to understand how the agent reached that answer. Did the agent use the correct tools? Did it interact efficiently with the environment? We can validate certain tool calls, check for intermediate solutions in the trajectory, and look at how many turns / tokens were used. Verifying intermediate trajectory states is common in agentic evaluation. If the agent solves a task, then this provides a valuable signal. But, what do we do if the agent solves a small ratio of tasks in a benchmark? In this case, we need to have a more granular measure of performance that allows us to understand how close the agent came to solving certain problems. Agent evals are expensive. Unlike traditional LLM benchmarks, agent evaluations can span long time horizons with many reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment interactions. A single evaluation may require vast amounts of generated tokens and dozens or hundreds of interaction turns with the environment. For this reason, agent evaluations are much more difficult to both curate and run! This data is super complex and even solving a single task can be expensive. Less data, more noise. Because each evaluation is costly, we typically run far fewer examples than in traditional LLM benchmarks. This is both because each task can take a long time to run and because curating the data / setup for each task is expensive. Rather than evaluating single dataset examples, we are asking the agent to solve a real problem. As a result, we usually have smaller evaluation dataset with higher variance, making reliable measurement difficult. — https://nitter.net/cwolferesearch/status/2083588813675274301#m

Is exceptional growth meaningfully predictable, or is it largely an emergent, path-dependent outcome that can only be detected after it begins? Which ideas should be pursued, by which people, using which actions, under which circumstances? When should they stop? What skills can we teach that meaningfully improve entrepreneurial success? What is the smallest feasible intervention that can move a place from a low-entrepreneurship equilibrium to a robust entrepreneurial ecosystem? What processes cause some firms to become less adaptable as they grow while others stay flexible? Which elements of other firms must a startup imitate and which may it violate?

Your model router charges you for context that you've already paid for, eleven times over. Prompt caches belong to one model. Change the model during a session, and the new model will read everything all over again, at the full price. We priced it with three different session sizes. Same 12 turns, run five times. > One switch cost 11x warm > Routing somewhere else cost 47% more > Caches don't transfer between models Grok 4.5 gives output five times cheaper than the model it took over from. Price change was 0.2% in one test, and 7.9% in another. The second issue is hidden under all of that. Claude counts 58% more tokens than GPT for the same prompt. So, spending $2 instead of $5 is not a 60% savings. On the same prompt, it's closer to 37%. Which part owns the decision on which model to use?, When will a switch ever become profitable?, And why does it become even more expensive with longer runs?

processed.summary: Cette journée a été riche en annonces majeures et en réflexions profondes sur l'IA. De nouveaux modèles puissants, capables de résoudre des problèmes mathématiques complexes ou de donner une "intelligence corporelle" aux robots, ont été lancés, souvent avec des réductions de coûts significatives. Parallèlement, le débat sur la sécurité, la régulation et l'accès aux modèles d'IA, qu'ils soient ouverts ou propriétaires, s'est intensifié, notamment suite à des incidents de sécurité. Des outils pratiques et des astuces pour exploiter le potentiel de l'IA dans la vie quotidienne et professionnelle ont également été partagés, témoignant de l'accélération de l'adoption de l'IA.

glossaire.definition: Un programme informatique très avancé, entraîné sur d'énormes quantités de texte, capable de comprendre, générer et répondre à des requêtes en langage humain de manière étonnamment cohérente.
Un système d'IA capable non seulement de répondre, mais aussi d'agir dans un environnement, d'utiliser des outils et de planifier des tâches complexes pour atteindre un objectif.
Un modèle d'IA dont le code et les 'poids' internes (les informations apprises) sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de l'étudier, de le modifier et de l'utiliser.

Le processus par lequel un modèle d'IA utilise ce qu'il a appris pour faire des prédictions ou générer des réponses à de nouvelles données (par opposition à l'entraînement, qui est l'apprentissage initial).
La plus petite unité de texte que les modèles d'IA traitent, comme un mot ou une partie de mot, utilisée pour mesurer la longueur des entrées et des sorties et calculer les coûts.

Une technique malveillante où un utilisateur manipule un modèle d'IA avec des instructions spécifiques pour le forcer à contourner ses règles de sécurité ou à révéler des informations confidentielles.

Un cadre ou un ensemble d'outils qui entoure un modèle d'IA, lui permettant d'interagir avec l'extérieur (appeler des fonctions, lire des fichiers, naviguer sur le web) pour réaliser des tâches plus complexes.

category_summaries.actu: Aujourd'hui, de grandes annonces ont secoué l'univers de l'IA : OpenAI a révélé Astra, un nouveau modèle capable de résoudre des problèmes mathématiques complexes, et a réduit drastiquement les prix de ses modèles GPT-5.6. Google DeepMind a présenté Gemini Robotics 2, offrant une intelligence robotique avancée. Le marché des modèles ouverts s'est aussi dynamisé avec les lancements de DeepSeek-V4-Flash et Inkling-Small, démontrant des performances impressionnantes et une efficacité accrue. Enfin, des incidents de cybersécurité impliquant des agents IA soulignent la nécessité de tests robustes.
category_summaries.tips: De nombreux conseils pratiques ont été partagés pour mieux utiliser les IA : de l'importance de "raconter sa vie" à un LLM pour affiner sa compréhension à l'exploitation de ChatGPT Work pour automatiser des tâches récurrentes, créer des outils éducatifs interactifs ou même modéliser en 3D. Des astuces sur l'évaluation des agents IA et l'optimisation des coûts, en comprenant mieux l'efficacité des 'tokens' et le fonctionnement des 'harnesses', ont aussi été détaillées pour les développeurs.
category_summaries.idees: Le débat autour de l'IA s'est intensifié, abordant des questions clés comme la nécessité de tests tiers obligatoires pour les modèles d'IA avancés (Dario Amodei) et le rôle crucial des modèles 'open-weight' pour la cybersécurité et l'innovation (Andrew Ng, Jeremy Howard). Yann LeCun a souligné les différences de perception entre l'IA chinoise et américaine, tandis que François Chollet a exploré les limites de l'apprentissage profond et les futures voies d'évolution de l'IA. La question de la concentration du pouvoir de l'IA et de son impact sociétal (emplois, relations) a également été soulevée.
category_summaries.outils: Plusieurs outils et démonstrations innovantes ont été mis en avant. Perplexity a lancé son serveur MCP pour connecter des assistants IA, et son CISO a 'open-sourcé' Numbat, un outil de surveillance des agents de codage. Andrew Ng a présenté OpenWorker, un agent open-source capable de réaliser des tâches concrètes sur votre ordinateur. highlights.text_fr: Nous commençons à quitter le territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant, par exemple, de 'créer un SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo'. Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais curieux de voir ce que Opus 5 ferait si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget d'1 million de 'tokens' (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais un rendu 3D en JavaScript. Opus s'est lancé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (de manière procédurale) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais il est assez ahurissant que le LLM ait dû placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime le tout, et qu'il fasse même quoi que ce soit. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne prendrait le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l l'on passe de 'personne ne ferait jamais cela' à 'bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit'. Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper-personnalisés dans lesquels vous pouvez imaginer déposer des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière réflexion est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement vérifier leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux à l'intérieur d'eux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre très lentement et laborieusement des captures d'écran à différents moments, et il a commis quelques erreurs et créé pas mal de 'jank'. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore pas mal défaut. Vidéo
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne longue session de "divagation". Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus de détails pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime me pencher en arrière, passer en mode /voix et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, n'importe quoi, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, je le transforme en une petite interview de quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont en quelque sorte très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent, leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort un peu plus propre que ce que vous aviez au départ. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la fusion mentale et que vous avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
tips.decryptage: Pour mieux communiquer avec une IA comme ChatGPT, essayez de lui parler longuement en mode vocal, même de manière désordonnée. L'IA est étonnamment douée pour démêler vos pensées et vous aider à clarifier vos idées, ce qui rendra les interactions futures plus efficaces.

tips.text_fr: Excellente rédaction, les évaluations sont difficiles ! Voici 2 grandes catégories que nous utilisons pour évaluer les agents : 1. Mesurer l'état du monde 2. L'agent en tant que juge sur la trajectoire 1. Mesurer l'état de l'environnement avant et après que l'agent ait effectué la tâche. @harborframework et les évaluations conteneurisées facilitent cela. L'agent pense qu'il opère dans un monde réel et nous devons configurer ce monde (fichiers, outils installés, limites de sécurité, instructions) de manière à ce qu'il reflète ce que l'agent fera dans le monde réel. Chaque action de l'agent modifie le monde d'une manière ou d'une autre. Et le succès d'une tâche signifie l'exécution d'une étape de vérification sur l'état final du monde une fois l'agent terminé pour voir si cet état correspond à un succès. La difficulté ici est de calibrer quand l'agent produit un état final techniquement correct mais que votre vérificateur n'avait pas prévu - vous voulez souvent permettre cela ou vous assurer que l'état final correct est capturable par votre vérificateur. 2. Juger la trajectoire -> La justesse n'est pas le seul facteur - le coût, la latence, l'interprétabilité comptent aussi. Ceux-ci nécessitent de comprendre l'espace d'action. La bonne réponse est un bon signal, mais si l'agent y est parvenu en trichant, cela signifie que notre agent est mal aligné ET que notre tâche est mauvaise car elle permet la triche. Si l'agent est inefficace en termes de coût/tokens, c'est un signal que nous devrons peut-être lui insuffler plus de 'a priori' pour l'aider à trouver la bonne trajectoire (cela pourrait être une meilleure 'prompte').
tips.text_original: great write up, evals are hard! here are 2 broad buckets we use to evaluate agents: 1. Measure the State of the World 2. Agent as a Judge on the Trajectory 1. Measure the state of the environment before and after the Agent does the Task. @harborframework and containerized Evals make this easier. The agent thinks in operating in a real world and we need to set up that world (files, installed tools, security boundaries, instructions) such that it mirrors what the agent will do in the real world. Every action the agent takes alters the world in some way. And success on a task means running a verification step on the final state of the world after the agent is done to see if this state corresponds to a successful pass. The tricky thing here is calibrating when the agent produces a final state that’s technically correct but your verifier didn’t forsee - you often want to allow this to pass or make sure the correct end state is capturable by your verifier. 2. Judge the trajectory -> Correctness is not the only factor - cost, latency, interpretability matter too. Those require understanding the action space The right answer is a good signal, but if the agent got there by cheating the Task then that means our agent is misaligned AND our task is bad because it allows cheating. If the agent is inefficient with cost/tokens, then that’s a signal that we may need to imbue more priors to help it find the correct trajectory (could be better prompting) we’ll be doing a bunch more educational content and open sourcing our tooling, reach out if there’s anything you want to see in particular! this should be accessible and easy for every team to do! Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch) Why is evaluating agents so difficult relative to evaluating a standard LLM? An LLM generates a single response to a prompt. An agent instead interacts with an environment by reasoning, calling tools, observing the results, and repeating. Rather than evaluating a single output, we are evaluating a full trajectory for a long horizon problem. Outcome & environment. Success is usually determined by the final outcome. Instead of checking the agent’s output, however, we usually check the actual state of the environment after a trajectory completes. For example: - A coding agent can say it fixed a bug but still fail test cases. - A personal assistant could say “your flight has been booked!”, but we don’t know if this is true until we check the booking database. The environment plays a huge role in the evaluation process. For example, we need a stable environment that does not change over time in order to run reliable evals, and we need this environment to be efficient so that evals can be run efficiently. Additionally, the environment must be realistic and expose the proper harness / tools for the agent to be effective. Environment state. The final answer is only one part of the evaluation. We also need to understand how the agent reached that answer. Did the agent use the correct tools? Did it interact efficiently with the environment? We can validate certain tool calls, check for intermediate solutions in the trajectory, and look at how many turns / tokens were used. Verifying intermediate trajectory states is common in agentic evaluation. If the agent solves a task, then this provides a valuable signal. But, what do we do if the agent solves a small ratio of tasks in a benchmark? In this case, we need to have a more granular measure of performance that allows us to understand how close the agent came to solving certain problems. Agent evals are expensive. Unlike traditional LLM benchmarks, agent evaluations can span long time horizons with many reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment interactions. A single evaluation may require vast amounts of generated tokens and dozens or hundreds of interaction turns with the environment. For this reason, agent evaluations are much more difficult to both curate and run! This data is super complex and even solving a single task can be expensive. Less data, more noise. Because each evaluation is costly, we typically run far fewer examples than in traditional LLM benchmarks. This is both because each task can take a long time to run and because curating the data / setup for each task is expensive. Rather than evaluating single dataset examples, we are asking the agent to solve a real problem. As a result, we usually have smaller evaluation dataset with higher variance, making reliable measurement difficult. — https://nitter.net/cwolferesearch/status/2083588813675274301#m

tips.text_fr: Votre routeur de modèles vous facture pour le contexte que vous avez déjà payé, onze fois. Les caches de 'prompts' appartiennent à un seul modèle. Changez de modèle pendant une session, et le nouveau modèle lira tout à nouveau, au prix fort. Nous l'avons tarifé avec trois tailles de session différentes. Mêmes 12 tours, exécutés cinq fois. > Un seul changement coûte 11 fois plus cher > Acheminer ailleurs coûte 47 % de plus > Les caches ne se transfèrent pas entre les modèles. Grok 4.5 donne une sortie cinq fois moins chère que le modèle qu'il a remplacé. Le changement de prix était de 0,2 % dans un test, et de 7,9 % dans un autre. Le deuxième problème est caché sous tout cela. Claude compte 58 % de 'tokens' de plus que GPT pour le même 'prompt'. Ainsi, dépenser 2 $ au lieu de 5 $ n'est pas une économie de 60 %. Sur le même 'prompt', c'est plus proche de 37 %.
tips.text_original: Your model router charges you for context that you've already paid for, eleven times over. Prompt caches belong to one model. Change the model during a session, and the new model will read everything all over again, at the full price. We priced it with three different session sizes. Same 12 turns, run five times. > One switch cost 11x warm > Routing somewhere else cost 47% more > Caches don't transfer between models Grok 4.5 gives output five times cheaper than the model it took over from. Price change was 0.2% in one test, and 7.9% in another. The second issue is hidden under all of that. Claude counts 58% more tokens than GPT for the same prompt. So, spending $2 instead of $5 is not a 60% savings. On the same prompt, it's closer to 37%. Which part owns the decision on which model to use?, When will a switch ever become profitable?, And why does it become even more expensive with longer runs?
tips.decryptage: Cet article analyse un problème de coût caché avec l'utilisation des IA : lorsque vous changez de modèle d'IA au cours d'une conversation, les informations déjà traitées (le 'contexte') doivent souvent être repayées, ce qui peut rendre l'utilisation de plusieurs modèles beaucoup plus coûteuse que prévu, même avec des réductions de prix apparentes.

idees.text_fr: Il n'est pas temps de ralentir mais d'accélérer ! Les récentes cyberattaques alimentées par l'IA ont fait parler tout le monde des risques de l'IA. Nous devrions le faire. Mais ne perdons pas de vue l'ensemble du tableau ! Si nous y travaillons dur, l'IA rendra le monde plus sûr, et non moins sûr, tout comme la plupart des grandes technologies l'ont fait. Nous en avons déjà eu un aperçu : nous nous sommes défendus avec l'IA (plus précisément un modèle ouvert). Les mêmes systèmes qui ont aidé à arrêter une cyberattaque alimentée par l'IA peuvent maintenant aider à défendre contre des millions de cyberattaques chaque jour, tout en nous aidant à identifier et à corriger les vulnérabilités avant que les attaquants ne les exploitent. Pour y arriver, nous avons besoin de trois choses à mon avis : - Accroître la transparence avec le partage obligatoire des traces et la divulgation des incidents pour les cyberattaques par agent - Maintenir l'illégalité des cyberattaques alimentées par l'IA, avec des sanctions significatives pour les dissuader - Équiper les défenseurs de la meilleure IA, en particulier des modèles ouverts, pour réduire l'asymétrie des capacités entre attaquants et défenseurs. Si nous réussissons ces trois choses, l'IA ne créera pas seulement de nouveaux défis en matière de cybersécurité, elle rendra la cybersécurité fondamentalement et significativement plus forte. Et ce, avant de considérer l'impact de l'IA sur la science, la santé, l'éducation, la productivité, et bien plus encore. Il n'est pas temps de ralentir mais d'accélérer !
idees.text_original: It's not time to slow down but to accelerate! The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture! If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have. We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. To get there, we need three things in my opinion: - Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks - Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them - Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger. And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more. It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!
idees.decryptage: Yann LeCun argumente que malgré les risques de cyberattaques par IA, la solution n'est pas de freiner le développement de l'IA, mais de l'accélérer, en particulier pour les modèles ouverts, afin de mieux armer les défenseurs et de rendre la cybersécurité globalement plus forte.

idees.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be droit back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late.
idees.decryptage: L'"innovation sans permission" est l'idée que les créateurs devraient être libres d'innover sans devoir demander l'accord du gouvernement à chaque étape. Andrew Ng soutient que la protection de l'IA "open source" (ouverte) est essentielle pour maintenir cette liberté d'innovation face à une régulation potentiellement trop restrictive.

idees.text_original: The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

idees.text_fr: Les mathématiques retiennent beaucoup l'attention pour leurs problèmes non résolus, mais il y a des problèmes non résolus et importants dans de nombreux domaines qui pourraient potentiellement être abordés empiriquement, si l'IA devenait vraiment assez bonne. Des problèmes qui, s'ils étaient résolus, apporteraient une grande valeur à la société. Par exemple, j'étudie l'entrepreneuriat et certaines grandes questions non résolues sont les suivantes : Qu'est-ce qui cause le succès entrepreneurial plutôt que d'y être simplement corrélé ? Une croissance exceptionnelle est-elle réellement prévisible, ou est-elle largement un résultat émergent, dépendant du chemin parcouru, qui ne peut être détecté qu'après son début ? Quelles idées devraient être poursuivies, par quelles personnes, en utilisant quelles actions, dans quelles circonstances ? Quand devraient-elles s'arrêter ? Quelles compétences pouvons-nous enseigner qui améliorent significativement le succès entrepreneurial ? Quelle est la plus petite intervention réalisable qui peut faire passer un lieu d'un équilibre de faible entrepreneuriat à un écosystème entrepreneurial robuste ? Quels processus font que certaines entreprises deviennent moins adaptables en grandissant tandis que d'autres restent flexibles ? Quels éléments d'autres entreprises une startup doit-elle imiter et lesquels peut-elle violer ?
idees.text_original: Math gets a lot of attention for its unsolved problems, but there unresolved & important problems in many fields that could potentially be addressed empirically, if AI truly got good enough. Problems that, if solved, would bring large value to society. For example, I study entrepreneurship and some unresolved great questions include: What causes entrepreneurial success rather than merely being correlated with it? Is exceptional growth meaningfully predictable, or is it largely an emergent, path-dependent outcome that can only be detected after it begins? Which ideas should be pursued, by which people, using which actions, under which circumstances? When should they stop? What skills can we teach that meaningfully improve entrepreneurial success? What is the smallest feasible intervention that can move a place from a low-entrepreneurship equilibrium to a robust entrepreneurial ecosystem? What processes cause some firms to become less adaptable as they grow while others stay flexible? Which elements of other firms must a startup imitate and which may it violate?
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet propose de réfléchir aux "problèmes non résolus" dans des domaines comme l'entrepreneuriat, suggérant que si l'IA devenait suffisamment avancée, elle pourrait nous aider à trouver des réponses à des questions fondamentales qui freinent le progrès humain et sociétal.

idees.text_fr: Un agent solo fonctionne pour une personne. Étendez cette configuration à une entreprise, et vous créez une mémoire, des identifiants et des flux de travail séparés pour chaque employé. @viktor__com commence plutôt avec l'équipe. Il sépare la mémoire par équipe, sujet et tâche, puis connecte ce contexte à travers plus de 3 000 outils d'entreprise. Un client a utilisé Viktor pour vérifier les bons de commande, les conversations de livraison et les confirmations d'entrepôt à travers des systèmes séparés. Il a signalé une rupture de stock cinq semaines à l'avance. L'entreprise a déployé 12 flux de travail autonomes en 15 jours. Viktor maintient également les identifiants en dehors de l'environnement de l'agent : > Le code s'exécute dans un environnement sandbox restreint > Les clés API restent dans un coffre-fort crypté > Le contenu externe passe par des classificateurs > Les modifications de données nécessitent une approbation humaine. Sa mémoire partagée stocke les flux de travail, les corrections et les connaissances opérationnelles dans toute l'entreprise. Une autre organisation a commencé par la recherche de subventions. Viktor a ensuite développé 58 compétences opérationnelles qui ont pris en charge 10 plateformes web, deux applications mobiles et 27 automatisations planifiées. Une entreprise n'a pas besoin du même bot solo copié sur chaque ordinateur portable. Elle a besoin d'un agent d'équipe.
idees.text_original: A solo agent works for one person. Scale that setup across a company, and you create separate memory, credentials, and workflows for every employee. @viktor__com starts with the team instead. It separates memory by team, topic, and task, then connects that context across more than 3,000 enterprise tools. One customer used Viktor to check purchase orders, delivery conversations, and warehouse confirmations across separate systems. It flagged a stockout five weeks early. The company deployed 12 autonomous workflows in 15 days. Viktor also keeps credentials outside the agent environment: > Code runs inside a restricted sandbox > API keys stay inside an encrypted vault > External content passes through classifiers > Data changes require human approval Its shared memory stores workflows, corrections, and operating knowledge across the company. Another organization started with grant research. Viktor later built 58 operational skills that supported 10 web platforms, two mobile apps, and 27 scheduled automations. An enterprise does not need the same solo bot copied across every laptop. It needs a team agent.
idees.decryptage: Cet article distingue l'"agent solo" (pour un seul utilisateur) et l'"agent d'équipe" (pour toute une entreprise). Viktor est un exemple d'agent d'équipe qui gère des tâches complexes, partage les informations entre les membres de l'équipe et assure la sécurité des données, montrant comment l'IA peut être mise à l'échelle pour des besoins d'entreprise.

idees.text_fr: La course aux modèles ouverts ne consiste plus à trouver un modèle universellement "le meilleur". Apertus et OLMo de @allen_ai optimisent la transparence. Laguna de @poolsideai et @Alibaba_Qwen optimisent l'efficacité matérielle. Macaron de @Macaron0fficial transforme un modèle de base en un ensemble de spécialistes interchangeables. K3 de @Kimi_Moonshot , @deepseek_ai , GLM de @Zai_org et @MiniMax_AI poussent la capacité téléchargeable vers la frontière fermée. Cela change la façon dont vous devriez les comparer. > Un modèle peut être moins cher à exécuter mais plus difficile à charger > Un modèle peut être entièrement ouvert mais plus faible sur les 'benchmarks' > Un modèle peut être téléchargeable mais peu pratique à héberger > Un modèle peut être modulaire mais ajouter des échecs de routage. Une seule 'leaderboard' ne peut pas bien classer les quatre approches.
idees.text_original: The open-model race is no longer about finding one universally “best” model. Apertus and @allen_ai 's OLMo optimize for transparency. @poolsideai 's Laguna and @Alibaba_Qwen optimize for hardware efficiency. @Macaron0fficial 's Macaron turns one base model into a set of swappable specialists. @Kimi_Moonshot 's K3, @deepseek_ai , @Zai_org 's GLM, and @MiniMax_AI push downloadable capability toward the closed frontier. That changes how you should compare them. > A model can be cheaper to run but harder to load > A model can be fully open but weaker on benchmarks > A model can be downloadable but impractical to host > A model can be modular but add routing failures One leaderboard cannot rank all four approaches well.
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet explique qu'il n'y a pas un seul "meilleur" modèle d'IA "open-weight" (ouvert), mais plutôt différentes catégories de modèles qui excellent dans des compromis spécifiques (transparence, efficacité matérielle, spécialisation, puissance brute). Le choix dépend donc de l'usage que l'on veut en faire.

outils.text_fr: Nous commençons à quitter le territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant, par exemple, de 'créer un SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo'. Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais curieux de voir ce que Opus 5 ferait si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget d'1 million de 'tokens' (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais un rendu 3D en JavaScript. Opus s'est lancé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (de manière procédurale) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais il est assez ahurissant que le LLM ait dû placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime le tout, et qu'il fasse même quoi que ce soit. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne prendrait le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l l'on passe de 'personne ne ferait jamais cela' à 'bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit'. Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper-personnalisés dans lesquels vous pouvez imaginer déposer des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, ou etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière réflexion est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement vérifier leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux à l'intérieur d'eux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû très lentement et laborieusement prendre des captures d'écran à différents moments, et il a commis quelques erreurs et créé pas mal de 'jank'. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore pas mal défaut. Vidéo
outils.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video
outils.decryptage: Andrej Karpathy montre ici comment un modèle d'IA très avancé comme Opus 5 peut, à partir d'un simple texte, générer un monde virtuel complexe en 3D avec du code, même si l'IA manque encore de capacité à 'voir' et corriger son propre travail dans cet environnement.

outils.text_fr: Pour être vraiment utile, un robot a besoin de la dextérité que les humains tiennent pour acquise. Mais demander aux modèles d'IA de coordonner ces mouvements est incroyablement compliqué. Dans cette démo, nous avons poussé Apollo 2 à maîtriser la motricité fine et à accomplir des tâches ménagères délicates ↓ Vidéo
outils.text_original: To be truly useful, a robot needs the dexterity that humans take for granted. But asking AI models to coordinate these motions is incredibly complicated. In this demo, we pushed Apollo 2 to master fine motor skills and complete tricky kitchen chores ↓ Video
outils.decryptage: Cette démonstration met en avant la capacité d'Apollo 2, un robot contrôlé par Gemini Robotics 2, à effectuer des tâches nécessitant une grande "dextérité" (des mouvements précis et délicats), comme des tâches ménagères complexes en cuisine, ce qui est un défi majeur pour les robots.

outils.text_fr: Le travail d'équipe, c'est ce qui fait la différence. Pour tester la collaboration multi-robots avec Gemini Robotics 2, nous avons mis au défi nos robots Apollo et Duo de ranger un garage en désordre. Le modèle de raisonnement de haut niveau décompose ce qu'il faut faire, où aller et identifie le moment exact pour transférer le contrôle ↓ goo.gle/4h5N7CQ Vidéo
outils.text_original: Teamwork makes the dream work. To test multi-robot collaboration with Gemini Robotics 2, we challenged our Apollo and Duo robots to tidy up a messy garage. The high-level reasoning model breaks down what to do, where to go, and identifies the exact moment to hand over control ↓ goo.gle/4h5N7CQ Video
outils.decryptage: Cette vidéo met en scène la capacité de Gemini Robotics 2 à coordonner le travail de plusieurs robots (Apollo et Duo) pour une tâche complexe comme le rangement d'un garage, en gérant la planification et le passage de relais entre eux.

outils.text_fr: Beaucoup d'excellentes réponses et idées. Une de @marckohlbrugge que j'ai ajoutée s'appelle maintenant [ Remplir l'espace ] Si vous avez 2 clips et un espace entre les deux, il essaiera de générer une vidéo pour connecter les deux d'une manière ou d'une autre et la placera une fois qu'il aura fini de générer. J'ai aussi ajouté [ Régénérer ] sur n'importe quel clip si vous n'êtes pas satisfait du résultat et il le remplace également en place. Et [ Générer ] normalement sur la chronologie vous permet de générer à n'importe quelle position sur la chronologie. Édition vidéo axée sur l'IA ! Vidéo
outils.text_original: Lots of great replies and ideas One by @marckohlbrugge I added now called [ Fill gap ] If you have 2 clips and space in between, it will try to generate a video to connect the two in someway and place it after it's done generating Also added [ Regenerate ] on any clip if you're not happy with the result and it replaces it in place too And regular [ Generate ] on the timeline lets you generate on any position on the timeline AI-first video editing! Video @levelsio (@levelsio) All this talk about AGI destroying moats and everything made me want to ship again One of the conclusions from all of you was, if you can use AI to ship faster and better, you should just ship way more complex things, like things you could not imagine making before For me personally I'd never imagine making Adobe Premiere, Final Cut Pro or Capcut but on the web, it'd simply be too difficult for me, where do I even start? So today I just tried and vibecoded them into Photo AI! A fully functional video editor but the cool twist is this one can actually generate videos with you or your trained models in it directly in your video editor I'm personally less interested in the AI influencers etc, but more fun to make actual kinda cinematic short films with yourself and other people in it, so I made this Likeness in video models is now good enough so that gives lots of cool opportunities, but most AI platforms just let you generate 10 second clips but then you're stuck with that and have to put it together yourself in Final Cut Pro So now you can just [ Send to video editor ] inside Photo AI and you end up here And the next thing I'll add is the AI Agent sidebar I have in Photo AI's main app too, which lets an agent take control of the interface. In this case you'll be able to say "make a short film of me in Bangkok", it'll ask you some questions, then write a script of prompts, which are then generated as videos with you or other people as the actors in it and automatically edited into a short film on your time Then you can right click on any video you don't like (some videos just suck or have bad resemblance to you, shit happens), and click [ Regenerate], adjust the prompt a bit and the new video will show up in the same place on your video timeline In this case I did try to make a short film of me arriving in Bangkok as a digital nomad the first time and being dazed, lost and disillusioned as I am on the other côté du monde 🤯 Featuring Lorn's song "The Slow Blade" Video — https://nitter.net/levelsio/status/2083654998404268188#m
outils.decryptage: Pieter Levels a développé un éditeur vidéo basé sur l'IA qui permet de générer des clips vidéo et de les intégrer facilement dans un montage. Les fonctionnalités "Remplir l'espace" et "Régénérer" utilisent l'IA pour créer automatiquement des transitions ou remplacer des segments, rendant le processus de création vidéo plus rapide et accessible.
